title: Bounded decoding stride loop
statement: Let $m,d$ be natural numbers, let $\Lambda$ be a type of machine states, let $A$ assign an instruction to each state, and let an oracle assign a Boolean answer to each index in $\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$ and each bit string. Fix an input bit string $x$, four pairwise distinct register indices $\mathrm{ptr},\mathrm{base},\mathrm{acc},\mathrm{tmp}$ among the $m$ registers, an oracle index $j<d$, states $\mathrm{test},\mathrm{read},\mathrm{done}$ and state families $\mathrm{downs}(i)$, $\mathrm{copy}(b)$, $\mathrm{bump}(b)$, $\mathrm{clear}(b)$, $\mathrm{scale}(b)$, $\mathrm{take}(b)$, $\mathrm{add}(b)$, and $\mathrm{incs}(b,i)$, and a positive stride $s$. Suppose the instruction at $\mathrm{test}$ compares the pointer and base registers, proceeding to $\mathrm{done}$ if equal and otherwise to $\mathrm{downs}(0)$; for each $i<s$, $\mathrm{downs}(i)$ decrements the pointer, and $\mathrm{downs}(s)=\mathrm{read}$. The state $\mathrm{read}$ calls oracle $j$ in whole-input mode with the pointer register as its sole argument, proceeding to $\mathrm{copy}(1)$ on a positive answer and $\mathrm{copy}(0)$ otherwise. For either bit $b$, $\mathrm{copy}(b)$ compares the temporary and accumulator registers, proceeding to $\mathrm{clear}(b)$ if equal and $\mathrm{bump}(b)$ otherwise; $\mathrm{bump}(b)$ increments the temporary register and returns to $\mathrm{copy}(b)$; $\mathrm{clear}(b)$ clears the accumulator and proceeds to $\mathrm{scale}(b)$; $\mathrm{scale}(b)$ proceeds to $\mathrm{add}(b)$ when the temporary register is zero and to $\mathrm{take}(b)$ otherwise; $\mathrm{take}(b)$ decrements the temporary register and proceeds to $\mathrm{incs}(b,0)$. For $i<2$, $\mathrm{incs}(b,i)$ increments the accumulator and proceeds to $\mathrm{incs}(b,i+1)$, with $\mathrm{incs}(b,2)=\mathrm{scale}(b)$. The state $\mathrm{add}(b)$ increments the accumulator and returns to $\mathrm{test}$ if $b=1$, and otherwise proceeds to $\mathrm{test}$ if the temporary register is zero (or remains at $\mathrm{add}(b)$ if it is not). Let $w$ be a bit string, $B,k$ natural numbers, and let $v$ assign a natural number to each register. Assume that for every $i\le |w|$, the value of the binary suffix of $w$ starting at position $i$ is at most $B$; $k\le |w|$; every register value in $v$ is at most $B$; the pointer value is $v(\mathrm{base})+sk$, the accumulator value is the value of that suffix starting at $k$, and the temporary register is zero. Also suppose that for every $i<|w|$, the oracle answer on the encoding of $x$ paired with the binary expansion of $v(\mathrm{base})+si$ equals the $i$th bit of $w$ (using $0$ when that position is beyond the list). Then there is a register assignment $v'$ with all register values at most $B$, pointer value $v'(\mathrm{ptr})=v(\mathrm{base})$, accumulator value equal to the value of the entire binary list $w$, and temporary register zero; all other registers retain their values. Moreover, the machine reaches configuration $(\mathrm{done},v',\mathrm{none})$ from $(\mathrm{test},v,\mathrm{none})$ in finitely many steps, and at every step before arrival the configuration satisfies the stated precondition and all register values remain at most $B$.
hypotheses_covered: Natural parameters $m,d$; state type $\Lambda$; instruction function $A$ and oracle
Input bit string $x$; register indices ptr, base, acc, tmp are pairwise distinct
Oracle index $j$; states test, read, done and families downs, copy, bump, clear, scale, take, add, incs; stride $s$
Instruction equations for test, downs, read, copy, bump, clear, scale, take, incs, add, including their stated index and Boolean conditions
Bit string $w$; natural bound $B$; suffix binary values are at most $B$ for every $i\le |w|$
Natural number $k\le |w|$; register assignment $v$ with every value at most $B$
Initial pointer, accumulator, and temporary register values satisfy the stated equations
Oracle answers match the bits of $w$ for every $i<|w|$ on the specified encoded input
caveat: The formal conclusion and hypotheses are understood, but the long instruction schema and its operational details are unusually dense for a concise informal statement.
